Hostages
hõs'tə-jəz
n. pl. (persons held as security for the performance of terms; taken from Judah after a battle her king had provoked)
Old French hostage, from Latin obses, one given as a pledge. The Hebrew taarubah comes from arab, to pledge or give surety — the same root behind the word for a man who stands as security for another.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, at the end of a war Amaziah of Judah had picked: “And he took all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obededom, and the treasures of the king's house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria” (2Ch 25:24). Joash of Israel had warned him in a parable of a thistle and a cedar and told him plainly to stay at home; Amaziah would not hear, was beaten at Bethshemesh, and Jerusalem's wall was broken down four hundred cubits. The vessels of the house of God went north, and so did living pledges — men and boys held to guarantee that Judah would keep terms. The chapter says why the king would not listen: it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom. A pledge in Scripture is a solemn thing; the word's root is the same as that behind standing surety, and Judah, who had refused to be warned, ended by leaving her sons in another king's hand as the price of a war she chose.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a hostage as a person delivered to an enemy or hostile power, as a pledge to secure the performance of the conditions of a treaty.

expand to see more

HOSTAGE, n. A person delivered to an enemy or hostile power, as a pledge to secure the performance of the conditions of a treaty or stipulations of any kind.

2. Hostages were formerly given by princes as a security for the payment of tribute.

The treasures of the king's house, the hostages also. 2 Chron. xxv.

HOSTAGESHIP, n. The state of being a hostage.

Key Scripture

2Ch 25:24 — "And he took all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obededom, and the treasures of the king's house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria."

Pro 11:14 — "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety."

Pro 15:22 — "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established."

Psa 38:11 — "My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off."

Modern Corruption

The chapter is read as a story about a proud king, and its plainest lesson is skipped — that other people paid for what Amaziah refused to hear.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a leader's refusal of counsel is paid for by people who never sat in the room. Amaziah was warned by an enemy king, in a parable, and the warning was sound; he would not hear it, and the consequences fell on a broken wall, an emptied temple, and families whose sons went north as pledges. Scripture's two proverbs on counsel say the same thing from the other side — where no counsel is, the people fall, and in the multitude of counsellors there is safety — and both put the cost on the people rather than on the counsellor. That is the burden of office. A man who will not be advised is not merely risking himself.

There is a second thing in the account that repays attention. The Chronicler says the deafness came of God, that He might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because Amaziah had brought home the gods of Edom and bowed himself before them. Judicial hardening is a real doctrine and it appears in exactly this shape throughout Scripture — Pharaoh's heart, Sihon's spirit, Rehoboam's ear. It never removes the man's responsibility; Amaziah is blamed and punished, and the text does not present him as a puppet. It does mean that a settled refusal to hear correction may itself be a judgment already fallen, which is a sobering thought for anyone who finds warnings easy to dismiss. The mercy in the passage is small and real: the hostages are recorded. God noticed who was carried away for another man's pride.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew taarubah (H8594), a pledge or hostage, from arab (H6148), to give surety, to pledge oneself for another.

expand to see more

Hebrew taarubah (H8594) — a pledge, a hostage; the hostages also, and returned to Samaria; 2 Chronicles 25:24.

Hebrew arab (H6148) — to pledge, to become surety; be surety for thy servant for good; Psalm 119:122.

Hebrew erabown (H6162) — a pledge, an earnest; Judah's pledge left with Tamar; Genesis 38:17.

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel; the thing Amaziah refused; Proverbs 11:14.

Greek arrhabon (G728) — an earnest, a down payment; the Spirit given as the earnest of our inheritance; Ephesians 1:14.

Usage

"“The treasures of the king's house, the hostages also” — the price of a war a king chose."

"“Where no counsel is, the people fall” — the cost falls on the people."

"The hostages are recorded — God noticed who was carried away for another man's pride."
